extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of moral philosophy / classical ethics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts principles from Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics on what counts as the Chief Good (Happiness) and how human excellence (virtue) is constituted, acquired, and manifested. Useful for understanding criteria for a flourishing life and for evaluating moral character and action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chief Good / Final End
rubrics_metrics.description: The Chief Good is 'that for the sake of which the other things are done' — the end or object of pursuit which makes other activities intelligible and is chosen for its own sake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: health is the end of the healing art, victory of the art military, a house of house-building. Distinguish final from instrumental ends; some ends subordinate to others. The most 'absolutely final' is chosen always for itself and never for anything else.

rubrics_metrics.name: Finality and Absolute Finality
rubrics_metrics.description: A more final object is pursued in itself rather than as a means; 'absolutely final' denotes something always an object of choice in itself and never with a view to another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this notion to identify candidates for the Chief Good by testing whether they are sought merely instrumentally or sought in themselves. If multiple finals exist, prefer the most final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness is self-sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness (eudaimonia) is self-sufficient: 'that which taken alone makes life choice-worthy, and to be in want of nothing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-sufficiency is to be understood as adequacy for a complete human life (including family, friends, and community) but not infinitely extensible. Self-sufficiency helps distinguish the final good from partial goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function argument: Happiness as activity of the soul in accordance with reason
rubrics_metrics.description: The work (function) of man is a 'working of the soul in accordance with reason'; the Good of man is performing this function well — i.e., activity of soul in the way of excellence (virtue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies: as a good harp-player plays well, a good human performs rational activity excellently. Use this to evaluate whether a life/activity manifests distinctive human capacities (rational action) performed excellently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness as activity, not mere possession
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an important distinction between possessing a virtue (a state or habit) and exercising it; happiness is more properly a doing (activity) than merely an inactive state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A virtuous habit that is inactive (e.g., one asleep) does not by itself constitute happiness. Assess moral life by observed activity and functioning, not merely by dispositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration requirement: complete life
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness requires activity 'in a complete life' (ἐν βίῳ τελείῳ) — not a single day or short period but a full span sufficient to realize human excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not judge happiness from isolated episodes; evaluate across a sufficiently long and complete life to allow flourishing and the exercise of virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integration of virtues, pleasures, and intellect
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness typically combines moral excellences (virtues), intellectual activity, and pleasure; some hold pleasure or external prosperity contribute, but the core is virtuous activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different theories emphasize virtue, practical wisdom, or philosophical contemplation; Aristotle notes they may combine with pleasure and external goods. When evaluating a life, consider the mix of these elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure as inherent to virtuous activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure accompanies and is inherent in noble actions for the person who loves what is noble; it is not merely an added appendage but arises naturally from virtuous activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid treating pleasure as a mere external reward; for the truly virtuous agent, pleasure and noble action co-exist. Use this to differentiate authentic virtue from mere dutiful action lacking delight.

rubrics_metrics.name: External goods as instruments for happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain external goods (friends, wealth, political influence, good birth, beauty, children) are necessary to complete and enable many noble actions; their absence can mar blessedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat external goods as facilitating conditions rather than constitutive elements of virtue. Evaluate whether an agent has sufficient external means to act nobly; recognize constraints on flourishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness likely acquired via virtue and learning rather than chance
rubrics_metrics.description: While some may call happiness a divine gift or a matter of chance, it is plausibly achieved through virtue, learning, habituation, and discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments of whether happiness is teachable should consider the roles of education, habituation, and character formation rather than attributing it solely to luck or divine favor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion of non-rational beings and children
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-human animals and children are not properly called happy because they cannot perform the rational, virtuous activities that constitute Happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When attributing happiness, require the capacity and exercise of rational virtue; anticipate developmental constraints (children) and species differences (animals).

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability of happiness under misfortune
rubrics_metrics.description: A truly happy person will have a relative stability: virtuous activity makes one able to bear misfortunes nobly and to preserve character despite external changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate happiness by resilience and the capacity to maintain noble action amid ordinary misfortunes; recognize that only great and numerous misfortunes might destroy blessedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete virtue and appropriate end-of-life conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: To be fully happy one needs complete virtue and a life that is complete in duration; additionally, the manner of death and posthumous circumstances can factor into judgments about whether one was happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider life-holistic criteria (virtue across a whole life) and relevant end-conditions when judging whether a person is to be declared happy or blessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of human excellence: Intellectual vs Moral
rubrics_metrics.description: Human Excellence divides into Intellectual virtues (science, intelligence, practical wisdom) — largely arising from teaching and experience — and Moral virtues (liberality, self-mastery) — arising from habituation/custom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating character or education, distinguish which virtues are being developed: intellectual virtues require instruction and time; moral virtues require repeated right action and habituation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtues are acquired by practice (habituation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral virtues are formed by repeatedly performing the relevant actions: 'by doing just actions we come to be just; by doing brave actions brave.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Character formation depends on concrete practices and institutions (laws, upbringing). Evaluate moral formation by patterns of action and habituation, not by innate gifts alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: The doctrine of the mean: virtue between excess and defect
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral qualities are spoiled by defect and excess; virtue typically lies at a mean between two extremes (e.g., cowardice and rashness flank courage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess actions and dispositions for balance relative to right reason and circumstance. Application requires practical judgment; moral rules are not exact like mathematical rules and must be adapted to particulars.
